title: High-Q, high-power spin Hall nano-oscillators with thick NiFe layers enabled by SiC substrates
authors: Maha Khademi, Akash Kumar, Martina Ahlberg, Artem Litvinenko, Xiaotian Zhao, Saroj P. Dash, Johan Åkerman
abstract: Spin Hall nano-oscillators (SHNOs) are nanoscale microwave sources with potential applications in local spin excitation, neuromorphic computing, and oscillator-based Ising machines. Further improvements in output power and coherence are essential for these applications, and increasing the thickness of the ferromagnetic layer offers a promising route toward this goal. However, this comes at the cost of higher drive currents, which increase Joule heating and can degrade device performance. Here, we show that this bottleneck can be overcome by SiC substrates. By comparing otherwise identical W/NiFe nanoconstriction SHNOs on Al2O3, Si, and SiC, we find that the high thermal conductivity of SiC enables stable auto-oscillations in NiFe layers as thick as 10 nm, while the optimum performance occurs at 7 nm. The best SiC device reaches an average output power of 13.1 pW and a mean quality factor of Q = 23,000, representing the highest reported simultaneous output power and coherence for a single free-running SHNO. These results establish SiC and thermal substrate engineering as a route to thick-ferromagnet spintronic oscillators for coherent microwave generation in nanoscale devices.
summary: This work demonstrates that the thermal management of Spin Hall Nano-Oscillators (SHNOs) is critical for achieving high performance. By utilizing SiC substrates, which have high thermal conductivity, the researchers overcame Joule heating limitations, enabling the creation of highly coherent, high-power microwave sources compared to devices on traditional substrates.
main_problem: The primary challenge is improving the output power and coherence of Spin Hall Nano-Oscillators (SHNOs) by increasing the ferromagnetic layer thickness while managing the associated Joule heating.
main_result: Using SiC substrates, which possess high thermal conductivity, enables stable auto-oscillations in thick NiFe layers, achieving a record output power of 13.1 pW and a high quality factor of Q = 23,000.
method: The study combines electrical characterization (measuring power spectral density and resistance) with detailed thermal simulations using COMSOL Multiphysics.
model_or_system: The system involves W/NiFe nanoconstriction SHNOs fabricated on three different substrates: Al2O3, Si, and SiC. The performance is governed by spin-orbit torques and thermal dissipation.
key_observables: Average output power (P), mean quality factor (Q), threshold current (I_th), and temperature profiles.
important_parameters: Substrate thermal conductivities ($\kappa$): $\kappa_{SiC} = 450 	ext{ W/m}\cdot	ext{K}$ vs. $\kappa_{Al_2O_3} = 35 	ext{ W/m}\cdot	ext{K}$; optimal NiFe thickness found to be 7 nm.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the ability of SiC to effectively dissipate heat, preventing thermal runaway that plagues devices on lower-conductivity substrates.
figures_summary: Figures compare thermal maps and normalized resistance vs. current for devices on different substrates, demonstrating SiC's superior heat spreading capabilities.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares the performance of SHNOs on Al2O3, Si, and SiC substrates, first establishing the thermal limitations, then optimizing the ferromagnetic layer thickness, and finally concluding that SiC substrate engineering is the key to high-performance devices.
why_interesting: While this is a condensed matter spintronics experiment, the core concept of thermal management and optimizing device performance through substrate engineering shares parallels with controlling environmental coupling in open quantum systems.
